title: The `unsafe` package: what it allows and what it costs

videos.script: Go checks your types and your memory for you. The unsafe package is how you switch some of that off. This lesson is about what you get for it, and what it costs. {{sizes}} It starts with the harmless part. Three functions measure how the compiler lays a struct out in memory. The same five fields take thirty-two bytes in one order and sixteen in another, and a tool finds that for you. {{rules}} Then the pointer rules. An unsafe pointer is still a pointer to the garbage collector. A uintptr is just a number, and the object it names can be freed while you hold it. The documentation lists six patterns that are allowed. go vet catches some mistakes, and the race detector turns on a check that catches others. {{strings}} Next, turning bytes into a string without copying. In a benchmark it takes under a nanosecond, against nearly forty for the copy. It is also how a map of twenty thousand requests ends up with fifteen hundred keys made of other lines. {{cost}} Last, the bill. Unsafe code sits outside the compatibility promise. Its numbers change between machines. And its bugs print plausible answers instead of crashing. So the lesson ends with a rule for when it is worth it.
